h:
You’ve probably seen this circulating.

“The Bible never says Eve was made from Adam’s rib.”

Then comes the Hebrew.

The word is צֵלָע, tsela. Across the Old Testament, it usually refers to a side, flank, or structural side: the side of the Ark, the side chambers of the Temple, the side of a hill.1

The Hebrew observation is legitimate. The problem begins when people treat that observation as proof of much larger conclusions the text itself never makes.

I recently read two essays built on the same lexical point.

One claimed “side” uncovers a hidden Christ-and-Church pattern.

The other used it to prosecute Paul, the creation order, and two thousand years of Christian teaching about women.

Same Hebrew word. Two opposite Bibles.

When one broader word can supposedly prove both arguments, the word is not doing the proving. The theology arrived before the lexicon opened.

The context is anatomical

A word’s possible meanings do not settle its meaning in every sentence. Context narrows the range.

Genesis 2 describes a body.

Adam is placed into a deep sleep. God takes one of his tselaʿot. God closes the flesh in its place. Adam wakes and calls the woman “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”2

That is not a construction scene. It is a surgical procedure.

“Side” remains lexically possible. But “rib” is not some careless invention imposed on the Hebrew. It is an ancient contextual reading of what was taken from Adam’s side.

The plural matters too.

Genesis does not say God took “Adam’s side.” It says He took one of his tselaʿot.

The whole-side reading can answer that by imagining Adam as a complete being with two lateral halves, one of which God removed. Ancient Jewish interpreters proposed versions of that reading.3

But the verse itself never says Adam was double-sided, double-faced, or originally divided into two human halves. That structure has to be supplied.

A man having multiple ribs requires no reconstructed anatomy.

“Side” is available. “Rib” fits the scene without adding another story behind it.

Changing the word does not change the order

Tanner’s argument who is attacking Christian teaching needs the rib translation to carry far more weight than it actually does.

The argument runs something like this:

Bad translation. Bad creation order. Bad Paul. Bad Christian tradition.

But replace “rib” with “side” and nothing Paul says changes.

The woman is still formed after the man.

Still taken from the man.

Still built from what was taken.

Still brought to him.

Paul’s statement in 1 Timothy 2:13 is not:

Adam’s rib was formed first.

It is:

“Adam was formed first, then Eve.”

That sequence survives either translation.

So does Paul’s statement in 1 Corinthians 11 that woman came from man. The discomfort was never really about the anatomy. It was about the sequence and the fact that the woman was taken from the man.4

The rib reading gets attacked because the rest of the chapter cannot be translated away.

Genesis 1 never says “at the same moment”

The next argument is that Genesis contains two conflicting creation stories.

Genesis 1 supposedly creates man and woman together, at the same moment. Genesis 2 places the man first and the woman afterward. Therefore, the accounts disagree.

There is one problem.

“Same moment” is not in Genesis 1:27.5

The verse says God created mankind, male and female. It does not narrate the order of their individual formation. It says neither “together” nor “separately.”

That is silence, not simultaneity.

You cannot insert “at the same moment” into Genesis 1 and then accuse Genesis 2 of contradicting the words you added.

The straightforward reading remains clear: Genesis 1 gives the broad account of creation. Genesis 2 returns to the creation of humanity and narrates it in detail.

Overview first. Close examination second. A summary and its expansion are not rival testimonies.

Jerome did not invent Adam’s rib

The Bible Secrets essay goes further. It claims the rib reading only became fixed when Jerome translated the Greek pleura as the Latin costa in the Vulgate, turning him into the decisive figure behind the Christian tradition.

The timeline does not work.

The Greek Septuagint already used pleura, a word capable of referring to the bodily side or rib. The rib reading was available before the Vulgate.6

More decisively, Theophilus of Antioch was already discussing why Eve was formed from Adam’s rib in the second century, roughly two hundred years before Jerome.7

Jerome made the Latin anatomically explicit. He did not invent the interpretation.

The claim that Christian Europe inherited one man’s mistranslation manufactures a scandal the historical evidence does not support.

Typology does not prove anatomy either

The same essay moves in the opposite direction.

It takes “side” as architectural language, connects Eve being built from Adam’s side with the Church, and then links Adam’s opened side to Christ’s pierced side in John 19.

Sounds beautiful.

That does not make it the lexical meaning of Genesis 2.

Christ-and-Church typology may illuminate the passage. Paul himself connects marriage to Christ and the Church in Ephesians 5. But later theological correspondence cannot decide whether tsela means Adam’s whole side rather than a rib taken from his side.

Typology may grow from the text. It cannot rewrite the anatomy underneath it.

The Christ pattern does not require Adam to have been split into two equal halves. Christ’s side is pierced whether Eve came from a rib, a section of his side, or some larger portion of flesh and bone.

The theological connection survives without pretending the Hebrew settled more than it did.

Consequences do not determine meaning

Both essays eventually point toward what the rib reading has been used to justify.

Female inferiority. Women silenced. Church hierarchy. An all-male priesthood.

Those historical questions deserve examination. But they do not determine the translation. A true reading can be abused. A false reading can feel liberating.

“What has this passage been used to defend?” is not the same question as “What does this Hebrew word mean in this sentence?”

Mixing those questions creates moral pressure where textual evidence should be.

The text does not need to be rewritten to protect the woman’s dignity. She is called Adam’s own bone and flesh.

She is his ezer, a strong helper corresponding to him.

She is built by God and brought to the man as the answer to his aloneness.

Genesis is not thin on her worth. It simply does not purchase her worth by erasing the order of the story.

Conclusion

The Hebrew word tsela does not always mean “rib.” No one serious disputes that. But words are not translated from dictionaries. They are translated from context.

In Genesis 2, the context is unmistakably anatomical. Adam is placed into a deep sleep. God takes one of his tselaʿot. He closes the flesh in its place. Adam responds, “Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” The Septuagint preserved an anatomical reading. The earliest Christians inherited it. Jerome did not invent it. Paul never argues against it.

Modern writers are free to argue that “side” better captures the Hebrew. What they are not free to claim is that the familiar “rib” reading is a late mistranslation imposed on the text to support “modern patriarchy.”

The evidence points in the opposite direction.

Genesis is describing the removal of a rib. Modern sensibilities may prefer a different picture, but they do not have the authority to rewrite the scene.

Not everything that sounds profound is true.

Be slow to assume your favorite modern teacher has uncovered what the people closest to the text somehow failed to see.

Novelty is not evidence. The text still gets the final word.

The internet rewards hot takes.

Kingdom Code is building something slower.

Subscribe for future investigations, explore the growing Archive, and share this essay with someone who values Scripture over inherited assumptions.

1

The Hebrew noun tsela has a broad range including “side,” “side chamber,” “beam,” and, in Genesis 2, “rib.” The lexical breadth is real. The dispute concerns which sense the immediate context requires.

2

The Hebrew construction is אַחַת מִצַּלְעֹתָיו, “one of his tselaʿot.” The scene also includes sleep, removal, the closing of flesh, and Adam’s declaration of shared bone and flesh. These contextual details explain why “rib” became an ancient anatomical reading rather than an arbitrary mistranslation.

3

Genesis Rabbah preserves an interpretation in which the first human was created with two faces or joined sides and was later divided. This proves that the whole-side reading has an ancient pedigree. It does not prove that Genesis 2 itself explicitly describes an androgynous or double-bodied Adam.

4

Paul explicitly appeals to formation order in 1 Timothy 2:13 and to the woman’s origin from the man in 1 Corinthians 11:8. Neither statement depends on whether tsela is rendered “rib” or “side.”

5

Genesis 1:27 affirms the creation of humanity as male and female but does not state that the man and woman were individually formed at the same instant. Genesis 2:21–23 supplies the detailed sequence. Whether the chapters reflect distinct literary sources is a separate question from whether Genesis 1 explicitly teaches simultaneity.

6

The Septuagint renders Genesis 2:21 with μίαν τῶν πλευρῶν αὐτοῦ, “one of his pleurai.” The Greek preserves the plural structure of the Hebrew. Pleura can denote the bodily side or ribs, so the Greek did not eliminate the anatomical reading that Jerome supposedly introduced later.

7

Theophilus of Antioch’s To Autolycus, Book II, chapter 28, explicitly treats Eve as formed from Adam’s rib in the second century.

Jerome’s Latin later reads unam de costis eius, “one of his ribs.” The evidence therefore supports a narrower conclusion: Jerome made the Latin wording explicit, but the Christian rib interpretation clearly predates him.
